claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be prepared as a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase by rapid quenching.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a composition-dependent thermodynamic preference for ordering into B2.
The thermodynamic tendency toward B2 ordering is realized only when atomic diffusion is sufficiently activated.
Observable phase stability is governed by competition between thermodynamic instability toward ordering and diffusion-limited kinetics.
Intermediate-temperature annealing activates diffusion without necessarily allowing it to reach completion.
Increasing annealing time will reveal the onset and evolution of B2 ordering.
The structural mediator is nucleation and growth of nanoscale ordered B2 domains embedded in a disordered BCC matrix.
Sufficient intermediate-temperature annealing permits local atomic ordering through diffusion.
Ordering produces a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC.
The length scale and extent of the two-phase microstructure directly correlate with the degree of diffusion during processing.
Annealing conditions that allow substantial diffusion will cause progressive emergence and coarsening of nanoscale B2 domains.
Shorter anneals or lower annealing temperatures will leave the alloy primarily homogeneous BCC.
The degree of phase separation will scale systematically with annealing time and temperature.
The as-quenched baseline has no detectable nanoscale ordering.
The proposed diffusion-controlled mechanism applies within a critical intermediate-temperature window.
Below the critical temperature window, insufficient atomic mobility precludes ordering.
Above the critical temperature window, rapid diffusion may cause complete transformation or coarser phase separation.
Minor composition changes may substantially alter the thermodynamic and kinetic phase-stability landscape.

contradictions.description: The high-temperature BCC state is said to suppress ordering through kinetic limitations, while the boundary statement says temperatures above the intermediate window provide rapid diffusion. Thus the stated kinetic explanation for suppression in the high-temperature state conflicts with the asserted increase in mobility at high temperature.
